title: Hallertau Mittelfrüh and German Lager | Craft Beer School
desc: What makes Hallertau Mittelfrüh a classic German lager hop: its history, aroma and alpha, the beers it suits and how to use it on a commercial brewhouse.
teaser: Hallertau Mittelfrüh is the gentle, floral hop behind many classic German lagers. It nearly disappeared, which says a lot about how hops are farmed.
standfirst: Hallertau Mittelfrüh is one of the original noble hops. Its soft floral and spicy aroma is part of the character of classic helles, Märzen and German Pilsner. It is also a fragile, low-yielding variety, which explains why it became rare and why brewers still seek it out.
sections: Mittelfrüh is a landrace from Germany's largest hop region

The Hallertau is a hop-growing region in Bavaria, north of Munich. It is one of the largest hop-growing areas in the world. Mittelfrüh means middle-early, after the variety's harvest time. It is an old landrace, selected by farmers over generations rather than bred in a programme.

It is one of the four traditional noble hops, alongside Saaz, Tettnang and Spalt. Our guide to noble hops explains what the term means and where it came from.
It nearly disappeared in the twentieth century

Mittelfrüh is susceptible to Verticillium wilt, a soil-borne fungal disease. As wilt spread through the Hallertau during the twentieth century, farmers replaced it with more resistant varieties such as Hallertauer Hersbrucker. Later, German breeders released varieties such as Hallertauer Tradition, aiming for a similar aroma with better disease resistance and yield.

Mittelfrüh survives in smaller acreage today. It is grown by farmers who supply brewers willing to pay for the original. It is also grown in other countries under the Hallertau name, though climate and soil change the aroma.
The aroma is floral, spicy and quiet

Mittelfrüh is low in alpha acid, typically around 3 to 5.5%. Its aroma is floral and gently spicy, with herbal and slightly earthy notes. Some brewers find a light fruity edge. It is more delicate than Saaz and much softer than any modern American hop.

That delicacy is the point in German lager. The hop sits in the background, giving the beer a finished, refined character without competing with the malt. A drinker might not name it, but would miss it if it were gone.
It suits helles, Märzen and German Pilsner

• Helles: around 16 to 22 IBU. Mittelfrüh adds a quiet floral note to a soft, bready malt base. Our helles style guide covers the style.
  • German Pilsner: around 25 to 40 IBU. Drier and more bitter than Czech Pilsner, with a clear hop aroma.
  • Märzen: around 18 to 24 IBU. The hop is barely there, supporting a toasty malt profile.

A simple 1,000 litre helles at about 11.5 °P might use 95% Pilsner malt, such as Weyermann Barke Pilsner malt, with 5% light Munich malt. Add Mittelfrüh at the start of the boil for most of the bitterness, plus a smaller addition 10 to 15 minutes before the end. Adjust weights to the alpha acid on your certificate.
German lager depends on clean fermentation

A delicate hop only shows in a clean beer. German lagers are fermented cold with lager yeast, typically 9 to 12 °C, then lagered near 0 °C for several weeks. Warm fermentation adds fruity esters that mask the hop. Diacetyl, left from a rushed fermentation, smells of butter and covers everything. Our guide to lager yeast strains compares the common choices.

For Indian breweries, the challenge is keeping fermentation cold when ambient temperatures run well above 30 °C. Glycol capacity matters. A fermenter that drifts two degrees warm during the peak of fermentation will produce a different beer.

With a hop this quiet, everything else in the beer shows: water, malt, fermentation and lagering. That makes German lager one of the best teachers in brewing.
Water and freshness matter as much as the hop

Soft to moderate water suits these styles. High sulphate makes delicate hop bitterness harsh. Most brewers in India start from RO water and add small amounts of calcium chloride and gypsum to suit each style.

Mittelfrüh is also sensitive to storage. Its aroma is subtle, so ageing shows quickly. The floor detail here: buy a crop year at a time, store it frozen and taste a few pellets from each lot before brewing. A lot that smells flat or cheesy belongs in an early bittering addition, not the aroma one.
Close substitutes exist when stock runs out

Mittelfrüh is not always easy to buy in India, where most hop suppliers stock a short list of popular varieties. When it is out of stock, the nearest swaps are its German descendants and neighbours. Hallertauer Tradition was bred to give a similar aroma and is often the first choice. Hallertauer Hersbrucker is a little more herbal. Tettnang and Spalt sit close in character too.

None of them is identical. In a helles the difference is small. In a German Pilsner with a prominent late addition, a careful taster may notice. Adjust the weight for alpha acid, since Tradition usually runs a little higher than Mittelfrüh. Keep the rest of the recipe unchanged so you can judge the swap fairly.
Taste a helles with fresh eyes

Pour a fresh German helles and let it warm a couple of degrees. Look for a light floral note behind the bread and honey of the malt. That is the hop doing its quiet job. Then rub a few Mittelfrüh pellets and compare.
faqs: Is Hallertau Mittelfrüh a noble hop?
Yes. It is one of the four traditional noble hops, alongside Saaz, Tettnang and Spalt.
What does Hallertau Mittelfrüh taste like?
Floral and gently spicy, with herbal and slightly earthy notes. It is delicate and quiet compared with modern hops.
It is susceptible to Verticillium wilt and yields poorly, so many farmers replaced it with more resistant varieties during the twentieth century.
Classic German lagers, especially helles, Märzen and German Pilsner.
